# SK0243 — The qualifier is redundant

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A namespace- or type-qualified type name the simple name already binds to, or a `base.` that reaches the same member as no qualifier.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Cleanup |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `RedundantQualifier` (`resharper_redundant_qualifier_highlighting`) |
| Supersedes | RedundantBaseQualifier |

## Why

A qualifier is how a reader is told that the short name would have meant something else, so one that changes nothing is a false signal: `System.Text.StringBuilder` beside a `using System.Text;` says there is an ambiguity to resolve, and there is not. `base.` says louder still — it says the containing type has its own member of that name and this call deliberately goes past it. `SK0207` owns the `this.` qualifier and `SK0215` the static one; these are the two shapes the arrangement rules leave.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
using System.Text;

sealed class Formatter {
    System.Text.StringBuilder builder = new();
}
```

Write:

```csharp
using System.Text;

sealed class Formatter {
    StringBuilder builder = new();
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Neither half is decided by comparing text.** The type half asks the semantic model to bind the short name *at the same position* and reports only when it produces the same symbol with no candidates, which is what makes a shadowing type, a missing using directive and a genuine ambiguity each answer for themselves. Deciding it by looking for a matching using directive would be a different rule, and it would be wrong every time two imported namespaces offer the same name. ⚠ **The `base.` half is not "the containing type does not override it", and believing that is how this rule would report a behaviour change as a redundancy.** Given `class A { public virtual void M() { } }`, a `class B : A` calling `base.M()`, and a `class C : B` that overrides `M` — dropping the qualifier in `B` turns a non-virtual call to `A.M` into a virtual one that reaches `C.M`. So the member must be one nothing can override further (not virtual, not abstract, not an unsealed override) or the containing type must be `sealed`. Two further conditions: the containing type must declare nothing of that name, and nothing in scope at that position may be a local, a parameter or a local function of that name, because an unqualified use would find it first. ⚠ **An attribute name is left out.** `[System.Obsolete]` binds to a *constructor* rather than to a type, so the symbol comparison the rest of the rule performs would be comparing the wrong things; the shape is real and it is declined rather than answered with a check that does not mean what it says. ⚠ `global::` is a deliberate disambiguator and is never removed — a short name that binds to the same symbol today is exactly what somebody wrote `global::` to stop depending on. A qualified name inside another one's type arguments is skipped too, because the outer finding and the inner one would be two overlapping edits, and two overlapping edits are not a fix. Using directives, namespace declarations and documentation `cref`s are all positions where the written name *is* the meaning. ⚠ **`UnusedImportClause` belongs to `SK0210`, not here**, and so does `RedundantUsingDirective.Global` — shipping either here would have been a second rule for one concept. ⚠ The reason recorded against that decision was wrong and is withdrawn: it said `SK0210`'s removal set is Roslyn's CS8019 and that the global-duplication shape reports CS8933, which that filter does not read. The set is CS8019, but the shape reports **CS8019 as well as** CS8933 — measured across ten shapes, with the CS8019 set and the CS8019 ∪ CS8933 set identical in every one — so `SK0210` sees it and removes it, and there was never a gap here to decline.
